candidates.attacker_control: The `url` query parameter of the logout endpoint (`Pac4jConstants.URL = "url"`, read at DefaultLogoutLogic.java:88 via `context.getRequestParameter(...)`). No authentication or privileged state is required; a victim merely has to follow a crafted logout link.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the pattern is configurable and that passing arbitrary matching URLs is the intended mechanism (javadoc at DefaultLogoutLogic.java:27-28) — the issue is the mismatch between that intent and `//` matching `/.*`. Checked that the central-logout branch (lines 127-129) filters to `http`/`https` prefixes, so the protocol-relative value does not reach client logout builders. Checked DefaultUrlResolver.compute, which classifies non-http(s) values as relative and would not produce a scheme-relative result — the logout path does not use it, which is exactly why the raw value reaches the Location header. Checked that `HttpAction.redirect` performs no validation. This is the default configuration only; a deployment with a strict pattern (e.g. `^/[^/].*$`) would not be affected.
candidates.impact: Open redirect / phishing: an attacker can make the trusted application's logout endpoint send the victim to an arbitrary external site, which is standard phishing and token/referrer-leak primitive and defeats the documented intent that only relative URLs be accepted by default. Not demonstrated to be RCE or an authentication bypass.
candidates.prerequisites: The application exposes the pac4j logout endpoint (LogoutLogic/DefaultLogoutLogic, used by the framework integrations listed in the repository docs) and does not configure a stricter `logoutUrlPattern`; in that case the input pattern is null and the default `/.*` from Pac4jConstants applies. A victim must follow the crafted link.
candidates.root_cause: DefaultLogoutLogic takes the attacker-controlled request parameter `url` and, if it matches the configured logout URL pattern, passes it unmodified to HttpAction.redirect (Location header). The default pattern used when none is configured is Pac4jConstants.DEFAULT_LOGOUT_URL_PATTERN_VALUE = "/.*", which requires only that the value start with '/'. A protocol-relative URL such as `//attacker.example` therefore fully matches the pattern even though the constant is documented as meaning "only relative urls are allowed", and `Location: //attacker.example` is resolved by browsers as an absolute URL to the attacker's host.
candidates.title: Open redirect in DefaultLogoutLogic via protocol-relative URL that matches the default logout URL pattern
candidates.trace: 1) Attacker crafts `GET /logout?url=//attacker.example`. 2) The framework calls `LogoutLogic.perform(context, config, adapter, defaultUrl, null, ...)`, so DefaultLogoutLogic selects `logoutUrlPattern = "/.*"` (lines 50-55). 3) Line 88 reads the raw `url` parameter; line 90 evaluates `Pattern.matches("/.*", "//attacker.example")`, which is true because the whole string starts with '/'. 4) Line 91 sets `redirectUrl` to the attacker value; line 95 calls `HttpAction.redirect(context, redirectUrl)`, which sets `Location: //attacker.example` with a 302. 5) The browser treats `//attacker.example` as scheme-relative and navigates to the attacker's site. The same request-derived value is also forwarded to client logout builders for central logout (DefaultLogoutLogic.java:126-133), although the OIDC builder only uses it as `post_logout_redirect_uri` when it begins with `http`/`https`, so that secondary path is not reached by the `//` vector.
candidates.unverified: Not executed or reproduced; no runtime/integration testing was possible. The framework integrations that invoke LogoutLogic (spring-webmvc-pac4j, j2e-pac4j, etc.) are outside this snapshot, so I could not confirm every adapter passes a null pattern by default, though the library default in Pac4jConstants/DefaultLogoutLogic is unambiguous. Whether this exact defect corresponds to any particular published advisory could not be verified from the snapshot.

coverage_summary: Source scope: 647 root files, 590 model-visible; 57 files excluded as sensitive-name/path (path names containing \"credentials\"/\"password\", plus tests); binary-like files skipped. I read and traced the pac4j-core engine (DefaultSecurityLogic, DefaultCallbackLogic, DefaultLogoutLogic, decisions), authorization checker/authorizers (including CSRF and CORS), matching, profile/profile-service and serialization utilities, HTTP clients, CAS client/configuration/logout, OAuth/OIDC configuration, redirect and logout action builders, JWT signature/encryption configuration, and the pac4j-saml response validator, replay cache, SOAP/artifact-binding pipeline and redirect/POST transports. I did not fully read the large SAML2Configuration, SAML2MetadataGenerator, Pac4jHTTPArtifactDecoder, all OAuth provider profile definitions, or any excluded credential accumulator/authenticator files (unreadable). P1 index was used for navigation only (5799 symbols, syntactic call/containment edges; no dataflow, reachability or exploitability proof).
limitations: 57 files (paths containing "credentials" or "password", plus tests) are not readable in either B0 or P1, so credential extraction/validation code (e.g. OAuth/OIDC state checks in extractors, JwtAuthenticator, password encoders) could not be verified against source text.
No test sources are present in the visible tree; no build, tests, or scanners were run, so nothing is runtime-confirmed.

Framework integrations (spring-webmvc-pac4j, j2e-pac4j, etc.) that call the engine with concrete `logoutUrlPattern`/`client`/`authorizer` values live outside this snapshot; default-value behavior was inferred from pac4j-core only.

The P1 relation index is syntactic navigation (calls/containment facts) and does not prove data flow, reachability or exploitability; several large SAML/OAuth files were skimmed rather than exhaustively audited.
The snapshot's exact upstream commit date could not be determined (no VCS metadata), so correlation with any specific fix release or advisory was not possible from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: pac4j-core/src/main/java/org/pac4j/core/authorization/authorizer/CheckProfileTypeAuthorizer.java:33 — `return profile.getClass().isAssignableFrom(element);` reverses the expected assignability direction, so a profile of a supertype (e.g. a plain CommonProfile) passes a check configured for a concrete subtype (e.g. FacebookProfile), a potential authorization bypass.
rejected_leads.reason: Real logical inversion with plausible security impact, but exploitability depends on how the authorizer is configured and which profile classes an attacker can obtain, and I could not establish from the snapshot whether this is long-standing upstream behavior rather than an introduced defect. Kept as an unconfirmed lead, not a submitted candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: pac4j-core/src/main/java/org/pac4j/core/util/JavaSerializationHelper.java:26-31 plus InternalAttributeHandler.java:94-95 / UserProfile.java:443-450 — broad default `trustedPackages` (java., javax., org.pac4j., com.nimbusds., org.opensaml., net.minidev.json., …) used when deserializing session/attribute/profile data.
rejected_leads.reason: Only exploitable if an attacker can supply the serialized bytes (e.g. IdP/claim-controlled attribute value prefixed with `{#sb64}` or a shared profile store) and a usable gadget exists in the allow-listed packages; neither condition is demonstrated in the snapshot, so this remains a hardening/deserialization-risk lead.

Browsers reject `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` combined with credentials, and the CORS authorizer is only used when the caller explicitly requests `allowAjaxRequests`; no concrete cross-origin impact was evidenced.

rejected_leads.lead: pac4j-core/src/main/java/org/pac4j/core/redirect/RedirectAction.java:49-72 — `RedirectAction.post` HTML-escapes only location and data keys, not data values (`entry.getValue()`), with an escaper that also omits single quotes.
rejected_leads.reason: The helper is not referenced anywhere else in the snapshot, so there is no in-repo attacker-controlled path; impact is caller-dependent (potential HTML injection).

rejected_leads.lead: pac4j-core/src/main/java/org/pac4j/core/matching/PathMatcher.java:76-96 combined with J2EContext.getPath() (J2EContext.java:229-242) using the raw `getRequestURI()` for security matching.
rejected_leads.reason: A path-normalization mismatch (e.g. encoded/semicolon variants) is a plausible container-dependent auth bypass, but I could not verify any concrete browser/container combination from source alone; speculative.

rejected_leads.lead: pac4j-ldap/src/main/java/org/pac4j/ldap/profile/service/LdapProfileService.java:165 — search filter built as `key + "=" + value` without LDAP escaping.
rejected_leads.reason: The value originates from server-side profile lookups (findById/findByLinkedId) rather than a demonstrated request-controlled flow, so attacker control is not established.

summary: Reviewed the assigned pac4j 3.8.2-SNAPSHOT source tree (multi-module Java authentication/authorization library). I traced the engine/authorizer/matching paths, logout and callback redirection, SAML response validation and artifact/redirect transport, OIDC/JWT configuration, CAS, HTTP/OAuth clients and profile services. The strongest single source-evidenced issue is an open redirect in `DefaultLogoutLogic`: the request-controlled `url` parameter is only checked with `Pattern.matches(logoutUrlPattern, url)`, and the default pattern `"/.*"` (documented as meaning “only relative urls are allowed”) also matches protocol-relative URLs such as `//attacker.example`, which are then emitted verbatim as the `Location` header by `HttpAction.redirect`. No runtime confirmation was performed; alternative leads (reversed `isAssignableFrom` in `CheckProfileTypeAuthorizer`, broad Java-deserialization allow-list in `JavaSerializationHelper`, permissive CORS defaults, weak escaping in `RedirectAction.post`, LDAP filter concatenation) are recorded as rejected/unconfirmed rather than additional candidates.
